name: Eigenvector
meaning: A nonzero vector whose direction stays the same under an operator.

check.prompt: Can the zero vector be an eigenvector?
check.explanation: Nonzero is part of the definition.

name: Eigenvalue
meaning: The factor by which an operator scales an eigenvector.
formal: If $A|v\rangle=\lambda|v\rangle$ for nonzero $|v\rangle$, then $\lambda$ is its eigenvalue.
linkedFormal: If $A|v\rangle=\lambda|v\rangle$ for nonzero $|v\rangle$, then $\lambda$ is its eigenvalue.

name: Degeneracy
meaning: Several independent eigenvectors share the same eigenvalue.
formal: An eigenvalue is degenerate if its eigenspace, the set of its eigenvectors together with zero, has dimension greater than 1.
example: $A=2I$ on $\mathbb C^2$ has eigenvalue 2 with degeneracy 2.

check.prompt: For $2I$ in two dimensions, the degeneracy of 2 is…

linkedFormal: An [[Eigenvalue|eigenvalue]] is degenerate if its [[Eigenspace|eigenspace]], the [[Set|set]] of its [[Eigenvector|eigenvectors]] together with zero, has [[Dimension|dimension]] greater than 1.

name: Simultaneous Eigenvectors
meaning: Vectors that are eigenvectors of both operators.
formal: Finite-dimensional commuting Hermitian operators admit a common orthonormal eigenbasis. A nondegenerate eigenvector of $A$ is also an eigenvector of $B$; within a degenerate eigenspace choose a basis diagonalizing $B$. Commutation alone does not give this result for arbitrary defective operators.
example: Two diagonal matrices share the coordinate basis.

check.prompt: With degeneracy, does every eigenvector of A automatically diagonalize B?
options: No; choose a common basis within each eigenspace
check.explanation: B may mix vectors inside a degenerate eigenspace.

linkedFormal: [[Dimension|Finite-dimensional]] [[Commutator|commuting]] [[Hermitian Operator|Hermitian]] operators admit a common [[Orthonormal Basis|orthonormal eigenbasis]]. A nondegenerate [[Eigenvector|eigenvector]] of $A$ is also an [[Eigenvector|eigenvector]] of $B$; within a [[Degeneracy|degenerate]] [[Eigenspace|eigenspace]] choose a [[Basis|basis]] diagonalizing $B$. Commutation alone does not give this result for arbitrary defective operators.

name: Projection Operator
meaning: An operator that keeps a selected component of a vector.

check.explanation: It takes an overlap and rebuilds that direction.

name: Spectral Theorem
meaning: A finite Hermitian matrix has a complete orthonormal set of eigenvectors.
formal: For an $n\times n$ Hermitian matrix, there is an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues and $A=\sum_j\lambda_j|j\rangle\langle j|$. In infinite dimensions a self-adjoint operator has a spectral measure; normalizable eigenvectors need not form a discrete basis.

check.prompt: Does every infinite-dimensional observable have a discrete normalizable eigenbasis?
options: No; a continuous spectrum may occur
Only if its eigenvalues are real
check.explanation: Position is a standard continuous-spectrum example.

linkedFormal: For an $n\times n$ [[Hermitian Operator|Hermitian matrix]], there is an [[Orthonormal Basis|orthonormal eigenbasis]] with real [[Eigenvalue|eigenvalues]] and $A=\sum_j\lambda_j|j\rangle\langle j|$. In infinite dimensions a [[Self-adjoint Operator|self-adjoint operator]] has a spectral measure; [[Normalization|normalizable]] [[Eigenvector|eigenvectors]] need not form a discrete [[Basis|basis]].

name: Eigenspace
meaning: All vectors having a chosen eigenvalue, with the zero vector included.
formal: The eigenspace for $\lambda$ is $E_\lambda=\{v:Av=\lambda v\}$. It is a vector space; its nonzero members are eigenvectors.

check.explanation: The subspace includes zero although an eigenvector must be nonzero.

linkedFormal: The eigenspace for $\lambda$ is $E_\lambda=\{v:Av=\lambda v\}$. It is a [[Vector Space|vector space]]; its nonzero members are [[Eigenvector|eigenvectors]].

name: Multiplicity
meaning: The number of times a value appears as a repeated polynomial root.
formal: Algebraic multiplicity of an eigenvalue is its multiplicity as a root of $\det(A-\lambda I)$. For Hermitian matrices it equals the dimension of the eigenspace.
example: For $2I$ in two dimensions, $(2-\lambda)^2$ gives multiplicity 2.
linkedFormal: Algebraic multiplicity of an [[Eigenvalue|eigenvalue]] is its multiplicity as a [[Polynomial Root|root]] of $\det(A-\lambda I)$. For [[Hermitian Operator|Hermitian]] matrices it equals the [[Dimension|dimension]] of the [[Eigenspace|eigenspace]].

name: Spectrum
meaning: The set of values where subtracting that value times identity does not have a suitable inverse.
formal: For a finite matrix, the spectrum is its set of eigenvalues. In infinite dimensions, the spectrum includes continuous values where the inverse fails to be a bounded operator defined on the whole space; bounded means the output norm is at most a fixed constant times the input norm.
example: Position on the real line has continuous spectrum, not a discrete normalizable eigenbasis.

check.prompt: In finite dimensions, the spectrum is…
options: The diagonal of every basis representation
check.explanation: In infinite dimensions there can also be continuous parts.

linkedFormal: For a finite [[Matrix|matrix]], the spectrum is its [[Set|set]] of [[Eigenvalue|eigenvalues]]. In infinite dimensions, the spectrum includes [[Continuity|continuous]] values where the [[Inverse Matrix|inverse]] fails to be a bounded [[Linear Operator|operator]] defined on the whole [[Mathematical Space|space]]; bounded means the output [[Norm|norm]] is at most a fixed constant times the input [[Norm|norm]].
